To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the frequency of neutral sequence variants at a 150 kb locus on chromosome 11q is similar in chromosomes that contain a disease-causing mutation and those that do not.

the A-T mutation frequency in a population cannot be estimated from neutral sequence variants at this locus and that the use of single nucleotide polymorphic variants to identify loci that predispose to common diseases may be limited by extensive linkage disequilibrium and by the presence of common haplotypes.

(1) the A-T gene has 9 common neutral sequence variants in the coding and splicing regions of the gene; (2) these variants occur on both A-T and normal chromosomes; and (3) these variants are in linkage disequilibrium and fall into 7 haplotyes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis of disease and the development of genetic tests.
the identification of genes involved in the development of human diseases.
the development of methods to identify and characterize genes that predispose to common diseases, such as heart disease and cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the A-T gene is a very large gene with many common polymorphisms that are in strong LD.
the neutral variants and the A-T disease-causing mutations are in linkage disequilibrium.
there was no significant correlation between neutral variants and disease causing mutations at the A-T gene.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 9 SNPs in the A-T gene region were not useful for genetic association studies.
we found 9 common neutral sequence variants at this locus.
there is a lot of genetic variability in the A-T locus but that the mutations that cause disease are not associated with the variability.
The main takeaway from our work is that

SNPs in the coding and intron regions of a locus are not sufficient for mapping disease susceptibility loci, and that a more extensive SNP survey of the entire locus is necessary to identify haplotypes that are associated with a disease phenotype.
the A-T locus has a relatively small number of haplotypes that are in linkage disequilibrium.
the A-T locus is a complex locus, with many different haplotypes.
